name: Improved Holland Gin Cocktail
description: Genever with maraschino, absinthe and bitters. The Old Fashioned before anyone thought to call it old.
funFact: Improved meant one thing precisely in the old books: a plain spirit-sugar-bitters cocktail with maraschino and absinthe added, and nothing else.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Fancy Brandy Cocktail
description: Brandy, curaçao, sugar and bitters served in a sugar-rimmed glass. Fancy meant the rim, and nothing more.
funFact: Jerry Thomas separates plain, improved and fancy versions of the same drink; fancy adds only a sugared rim and a fine lemon twist, and costs more.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.
recipe.garnish: A lemon twist over a sugared rim

name: Absinthe Cocktail
description: Absinthe, water, sugar and bitters, stirred cold. The absinthe drip served as a cocktail rather than a ritual.
funFact: New Orleans drank more absinthe per head than any American city, and the Old Absinthe House on Bourbon Street still has the marble fountains it was dripped from.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Rum Old Fashioned
description: Aged rum, sugar and bitters. The template holds with any brown spirit, and rum takes to it better than most.
funFact: Demerara sugar syrup rather than plain is the one change worth making — it meets the molasses in the rum instead of sitting on top of it.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Morning Glory
description: Brandy and Scotch together, with curaçao, absinthe and bitters. Built to be drunk in the morning, which explains a great deal.
funFact: Nineteenth-century bar books have a whole category of morning drinks, and the honest reading is that they were hangover cures with better names.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Artillery
description: Gin and sweet vermouth with two dashes of Angostura. A Gin and It with the bitters that make it a cocktail.
funFact: The 1806 definition — spirits, sugar, water and bitters — means a drink without bitters is technically not a cocktail at all, which is the joke this one is built on.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Diki Diki
description: Applejack, Swedish punsch and grapefruit. Named for a Filipino chief the Savoy's bartender had read about.
funFact: Swedish punsch turns up all over the Savoy book and almost nowhere since — it was the fashionable bottle of the 1920s and then simply stopped being ordered.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Deshler
description: Rye and Dubonnet with curaçao and Peychaud's. Named for a boxer who never lost a fight he was paid to win.
funFact: It is named for the featherweight Dave Deshler, and it is one of very few pre-Prohibition drinks that calls for Peychaud's outside New Orleans.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Frisco
description: Rye with Bénédictine and lemon. Three ingredients, and the Bénédictine does most of the talking.
funFact: Bénédictine's label still carries D.O.M. for Deo Optimo Maximo, a monastic dedication kept on a bottle that a nineteenth-century wine merchant invented the backstory for.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Barbary Coast
description: Gin, Scotch, crème de cacao and cream. Named for the stretch of San Francisco you did not walk down alone.
funFact: The Barbary Coast was the city's saloon district until the 1917 vice raids closed it, and the drink outlived the neighbourhood by a century.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Suissesse
description: Absinthe shaken with egg white and anisette until it turns pale green and thick. A New Orleans breakfast.
funFact: Absinthe louches — turns cloudy — when water hits it, because the anise oils fall out of solution; egg white takes that cloud and makes it a texture.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin is painful to hold.
Strain into a small chilled tumbler, no soda.
Rest a mint sprig on the foam.

name: Café Brûlot
description: Coffee, brandy, spice and citrus peel set alight at the table and ladled while still burning.
funFact: The showpiece is the peel: a whole orange rind is studded with cloves and lowered on a fork so the burning brandy runs down it in a spiral of flame.

steps: Stud the orange spiral with the cloves and set it aside.
Warm the brandy, curaçao, sugar, cinnamon and lemon peel in a wide brûlot bowl or pan.
Light the spirit carefully and lower the clove-studded peel into the flame on a long fork.
Ladle the burning brandy over the peel until the flame dies down.
Pour in the hot coffee to extinguish it and serve in demitasse cups.
recipe.garnish: None — the peel is the theatre

name: La Louisiane
description: Rye, sweet vermouth, Bénédictine and absinthe. The house drink of a Bourbon Street restaurant that closed decades ago.
funFact: Restaurant de la Louisiane printed it as its house cocktail, and it sits between the Vieux Carré and the Sazerac in a city that produced remarkably few bad ideas.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Gun Shop Fizz
description: A whole bottle of Peychaud's stretched across twenty drinks with fruit, wine and soda. Bitters as the base spirit.
funFact: Kirk Estopinal built it at Cure in New Orleans around the idea that bitters could be a base rather than a seasoning; it uses roughly four ounces per batch.

steps: Muddle the lemon, orange and cucumber with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the Peychaud's, the red wine and ice, and shake briefly.
Pour unstrained into a Collins glass.
Top with soda and add more crushed ice to fill.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cucumber slice

name: Milk Punch
description: Spirit, citrus and hot milk curdled on purpose, then strained clear. It comes out looking like water and keeps for months.
funFact: Curdling is the whole technique: the milk solids trap the harsh compounds and the tannins, and straining them out leaves a punch that is clear, silky and effectively stable.

steps: Steep the lemon peels in the sugar for two hours to draw out the oils.
Add the spirits, water and lemon juice and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Heat the milk to just below a simmer and pour the punch into the milk — this way round, never the reverse.
Leave it to curdle for an hour, then strain slowly through a coffee filter until it runs clear.
Bottle it and let it rest; it improves for weeks and keeps for months.

name: Brandy Milk Punch
description: Brandy, milk, sugar and vanilla, shaken cold. New Orleans drinks it before noon and does not apologise.
funFact: It shares only a name with the clarified English punch — this one is opaque, shaken to order, and belongs firmly to brunch.

steps: Add everything to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds until it is properly cold.
Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice.
Grate nutmeg heavily over the top.

name: Claret Cup
description: Bordeaux lengthened with soda, citrus, cucumber and borage. The drink of an English summer afternoon on a lawn.
funFact: Cucumber and borage in a wine cup are not garnish — the whole style is built around cooling the drink and the drinker, which is what cup meant.

steps: Stir the sugar into the curaçao and brandy until dissolved.
Add the claret, lemon slices and cucumber ribbons and chill for an hour.
Set a large block of ice in a bowl and pour the mixture over it.
Top with cold soda water just before serving and float borage flowers if you have them.

name: Champagne Cup
description: Champagne stretched with brandy, curaçao and fruit over a block of ice. A cup rather than a cocktail, and served by the bowl.
funFact: Cups are always built over one large block rather than cubes — a block melts slowly enough that the bowl is still drinkable an hour into a garden party.

steps: Combine the brandy, curaçao, maraschino and fruit and chill for an hour.
Set a large block of ice in a punch bowl.
Pour the chilled mixture over it, then add the champagne slowly.
Top with soda water and stir once, gently, from the bottom.

name: Badminton Cup
description: Claret with cucumber, sugar and soda. Named for the Gloucestershire house, not the game — and the game is named for the house too.
funFact: Badminton House gave its name to both the cup and the sport, which the Duke of Beaufort's guests are said to have invented indoors on a wet afternoon.

steps: Put the cucumber slices, sugar and a grate of nutmeg in a bowl.
Pour the claret over and leave it to steep, cold, for one hour.
Strain out the cucumber and pour over a block of ice.
Top with cold soda water and serve.

name: Chatham Artillery Punch
description: Rye, brandy and rum under champagne. A militia punch with a reputation for ending evenings early.
funFact: The Chatham Artillery is a Savannah militia unit founded in 1786, and the punch's reputation rests on its habit of tasting like fruit and drinking like three spirits.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice, then stir in the cooled tea.
Add the three spirits and refrigerate for at least a day — it needs the rest.
Set a block of ice in a punch bowl and pour the mixture over it.
Add the champagne last, at the table, and grate nutmeg over the surface.

name: Mike Collins
description: The Collins built on Irish whiskey. Same lemon, same soda, a softer spirit underneath.
funFact: The Collins family is named once per base — John for whiskey, Tom for Old Tom gin, Mike for Irish, Pedro for rum, Pierre for cognac, Sandy for Scotch.

steps: Shake the whiskey, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Colonel Collins
description: The bourbon Collins, named for the rank the South gives anyone who owns a distillery.
funFact: Kentucky colonel is an honorary commission the state governor still hands out, and it has been given to distillers, astronauts and Muhammad Ali alike.

steps: Shake the bourbon, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Applejack Rickey
description: Apple brandy, lime and soda, with no sugar at all. A rickey is defined by what is missing.
funFact: The rickey was made at Shoomaker's in Washington for the lobbyist Joe Rickey, and the original was bourbon; gin only took over later.

steps: Squeeze half a lime into a tall glass and drop the shell in.
Fill with ice and add the applejack.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once. Add no sugar — that would make it a Collins.

name: Gin Buck
description: Gin, lemon and ginger ale. A buck is a rickey with ginger in place of soda, and lemon in place of lime.
funFact: Buck, mule and rickey are the same drink separated by mixer and citrus, and the names have been used interchangeably for a century by everyone except bartenders.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin and the lemon juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and hang a lemon wedge on the rim.

name: Whiskey Buck
description: Bourbon with lemon and ginger ale. The buck template on American whiskey.
funFact: Ginger ale outsold every other American soft drink through the 1920s, largely because it was the one mixer that could hide bathtub spirits.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the bourbon and lemon juice.
Top with cold ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with lemon.

name: London Buck
description: Gin and ginger ale with a squeeze of lemon. The buck named after the gin rather than the spirit type.
funFact: London dry describes a production method rather than a place — it can legally be made anywhere, and most of the biggest brands are not made in London.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the gin and lemon juice.
Top with ginger ale.
Stir once and garnish with a lemon wedge.

name: Mexican Mule
description: Tequila, lime and ginger beer in a copper mug. The Moscow Mule with agave underneath.
funFact: The copper mug was a marketing device from the start — it was the vodka distributor's idea in the 1940s, and it does genuinely keep the drink colder.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the tequila and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge and a mint sprig

name: Kentucky Mule
description: Bourbon, lime and ginger beer. The mule with the vanilla and oak of a Kentucky barrel behind it.
funFact: Bourbon must be aged in new charred oak, which is why it gives up so much vanilla so fast and why the barrels are then sold on to Scotland.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the bourbon and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge and a mint sprig

name: Nacional
description: Rum, apricot and lime from the Hotel Nacional, which has been pouring it since 1930.
funFact: The Hotel Nacional opened in 1930 and its bar survived the revolution intact — the drink is still on the menu, in the same room.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Isle of Pines
description: Rum, grapefruit and mint from the Cuban island now called Isla de la Juventud.
funFact: The Isle of Pines was disputed between Cuba and the United States until 1925 and is where Fidel Castro was imprisoned before the revolution he later won.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Gin Blossom
description: Gin, apricot eau-de-vie and dry vermouth, stirred and given a long stretch of orange peel.
funFact: Julie Reiner built it at the Clover Club in Brooklyn, and the eau-de-vie is doing something a liqueur cannot — it brings apricot without bringing sugar.

steps: Stir all ingredients with ice until very cold.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Cut a long strip of orange peel and express it over the surface.
Drop the peel in and serve.

name: Industry Sour
description: Green Chartreuse and Fernet-Branca with lime and sugar. Made by bartenders, for bartenders, at the end of a shift.
funFact: Joaquín Simó built it at Death and Co, and the name is literal — it is the drink the trade orders when the guests have finally gone home.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Trident
description: Aquavit, Cynar and dry sherry with peach bitters. A Negroni rebuilt from Scandinavian and Italian parts.
funFact: Robert Hess designed it as a deliberate Negroni analogue — same equal-parts skeleton, three substitutions, and nothing of the original left in the glass.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Slope
description: Rye, sweet vermouth and apricot. One of the Brooklyn drinks named for the neighbourhoods around the bar that made them.
funFact: Milk and Honey's staff named a whole run of Manhattan variations after Brooklyn neighbourhoods — Red Hook, Greenpoint, Bensonhurst, Carroll Gardens and this one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Fort Washington Flip
description: Applejack and maple with a whole egg. A flip built entirely out of things that grow in the northeast.
funFact: Chad Solomon named it for the Manhattan neighbourhood, and it is one of the few modern drinks to take the whole-egg flip seriously rather than as a novelty.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

name: Coffee Flip
description: Cold coffee, port and a whole egg. The Coffee Cocktail with the coffee it was always missing.
funFact: The classic Coffee Cocktail contains no coffee at all — it is port, brandy and egg, and it earned the name purely from how it looks in the glass.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a small chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg generously over the surface and serve.

name: Scorpion
description: Rum and brandy with orgeat and citrus, blended and served for several people out of one bowl.
funFact: Trader Vic's version is a bowl drink with a gardenia floating in the middle, and the flower is specified in the original recipe as seriously as the rum is.

steps: Put everything in a blender with crushed ice.
Blend on high for five seconds only — it should stay loose, not slushy.
Pour into a scorpion bowl or a large tiki mug.
Float a gardenia in the centre if you can get one.
recipe.garnish: A gardenia, or a mint sprig and an orange wheel

name: Q.B. Cooler
description: Three rums with honey, ginger, lime and orange. The drink the Mai Tai was reverse-engineered from.
funFact: Trader Vic tasted this at Don the Beachcomber's, could not get the recipe, and built the Mai Tai partly out of what he thought was in it.

steps: Flash-blend everything but the soda with a scoop of crushed ice for five seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tall tiki mug.
Add the soda water and top with more crushed ice.
Crown with a dense mint sprig.

name: Ancient Mariner
description: Two rums with grapefruit, lime and allspice. A modern tiki drink built to look like an old one.
funFact: Jeff Berry created it in the 1990s while reconstructing lost Don the Beachcomber recipes, and named it for the Coleridge poem rather than any bar.

steps: Flash-blend everything with a scoop of crushed ice for five seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tiki mug.
Fill to the top with more crushed ice.
Garnish with mint and a lime wheel.
recipe.garnish: A mint sprig and a lime wheel
